# Agents write weak copy: a lesson on Inkling

## Start

Agents are great at writing code now, but their copy is still weak. This is a short lesson on Inkling, a content writing framework for AI agents that fixes that. With Inkling, instead of writing the text right away, the agent first decides who will read it, then it writes tests for it, and it keeps editing until they pass. This flips the problem on its head, and gives the agent a way to work on writing just like it's used to working with code.

## Why AI copy is weak

But first, let's take a step back. Why do we need a content writing framework in the first place? Why is AI copy so weak?

Part of the answer is that code has a judge, and writing doesn't. When a model writes code, the tests pass or fail, and given the success of coding agents, those models were strongly trained with passing tests as the reward. A headline never fails a test, so the model stops once the text is accurate, and accurate is a long way from a stranger wanting to click.

And apart from that missing judge, our research found six main ways AI writing goes wrong: predictable words, conceding, the curse of context, poor theory of mind, formula punch and cramming. Let's go through them together.

## Predictable words

The first one is predictable words. A language model works by predicting the most likely next word. But good copy surprises you, and a surprise is an unlikely word. So, by default, the model's writing drifts towards the average of every marketing line it has read, producing something like a beige soup.

## Trained to concede

The second problem is that the model was trained to concede. Good marketing copy has to pick a side and argue for it, and that's a problem, because the model was trained to stay fair and balanced, so it softens every claim.

Say we're selling Instant Evals, a LangWatch feature, and we want to write "Instant Evals is the fastest way to understand your agent." That line picks a side, but the model writes "Instant Evals can be one of many helpful ways to understand your agent." It's fair and safe, but it gives the reader no reason to pick it.

## The curse of context

The third problem we call the curse of context, and it is very similar to what psychologists call the curse of knowledge. An agent that works for your company already knows your product, your plans and your internal words. So the agent writes as if the reader were inside the company too: no introduction, no context, and jargon like "ship the v2.4 fold behind ADR-150".

That line makes sense to the agent, and sometimes even to you. To anyone outside, it reads like Claudish, an ancient language only the model speaks.

## Poor theory of mind

The fourth problem, poor theory of mind, follows from the third. The curse of context is about what the reader doesn't know, and poor theory of mind is about who the reader is, because the model rarely stops to picture who is reading.

Poor theory of mind shows up like this: a brochure for a technical product has to convince a seller and an engineer at the same time, an order form has to satisfy a lawyer, and a pitch deck an investor. Each needs different words, but the model writes the same text for all.

## Formula punch

The fifth problem is formula punch, and you have surely seen it all over LinkedIn: lines like "It's not a tool, it's a movement", punchlines in threes, stacks of one-line paragraphs, and "And then it hit me". The model learned that these shapes look punchy, so it uses the same few again and again, and you spot them.

## Cramming

The last problem is cramming. When you ask an AI to write something, you hand it all your reasoning, and the model is eager to fit every piece in, because in code, dropping one requirement is a bug.

For example, I asked Claude for a bold headline against agent sandboxes, and it wrote: "Skip the sandbox: run your agents faster, safer and cheaper, with zero setup and full control." Everything I said is in there, so nothing stands out. Cut that crammed line down to one central idea and you get "You don't need an agent sandbox": one claim, and now you want to know why.

## How Inkling works

So how does Inkling fix all this? You give your agent the Inkling repository, in Claude Code or ChatGPT, and your agent follows a loop of four steps: decide who reads it, write the tests, draft and check, and let readers try it. First, the agent works out who will read the text and the one thing they should take away. Then it writes the tests: what a reader must be able to say afterwards.

Next comes the draft, and a style checker catches the patterns we just saw. Then a judge scores it. But a plain AI judge sides with the AI: researchers at Meta found it prefers AI writing up to 85 percent of the time. So our judge learned from lines a human approved and threw out.

Finally, pretend readers, like a busy founder, try to answer the tests. Once fresh readers get the main points, you stop editing.

## Recap

To sum up, one big reason AI writes weak copy is that nothing tells it when the copy failed. Inkling gives your agent that signal: decide who reads it, write the tests first, let readers with no context try it, and stop once they get it.
